title: Rust for Beginners
subtitle: Learn Rust from zero with a talking teacher and 13 hands-on labs that run real Rust in the app, including the ownership and borrowing errors
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A friendly, intuitive introduction to the Rust programming language in 13 chapters: hello world, variables and types, functions and loops, ownership, borrowing, structs, enums and match, collections, error handling, traits and generics, lifetimes, closures and iterators, and smart pointers with threads. Every chapter has a hands-on lab running on the built-in Rust Lab, a teaching interpreter that prints compiler-style errors (moves, borrows, lifetimes, exhaustive match) and shows an ownership log, with numbered figures, recaps, memory tricks, hierarchical concept maps and an exam. Programs run in a simulation of Rust, not the real compiler, so rare edge cases differ; the rules you learn are the real ones. The examples are our own, written in the spirit of The Rust Programming Language (MIT or Apache 2.0), which we recommend you read next.

summary: Rust is a programming language that gives you the speed of C with strong safety checks. The compiler is strict, but it is also a patient teacher: when it refuses your code, it tells you what is wrong and often how to fix it.

Rust programs are used for browsers, game engines, operating systems, command-line tools and web servers. Their big promise is that whole families of bugs, such as using memory after it is freed, are caught before the program ever runs.
In this chapter you write your first program, learn what println! does, and learn how to read a compiler message. Every chapter has a lab where you run real Rust right here in the app.

items: ELI5. Imagine you write a recipe and hand it to a very careful editor before it goes to print. The editor circles every mistake and says why. Only when the recipe is clean does it get printed. Rust's compiler is that editor, and the printed book is your fast program.

Now the real words. You write code in a file. The compiler, rustc, checks it. If it finds a problem it stops and explains. If not, you get a program to run. Cargo is the helper that does these steps for you. println! prints a line, and each {} is a hole for a value.
Try it. Run the first lab. Change Hello to your name. Then break the program on purpose by deleting a semicolon and read what the error says.
If you remember one thing: the compiler's errors are help, not punishment.

Think of the Rust compiler as a very careful editor. You hand it a manuscript. It reads every line before the book is printed. If it finds a problem, it sends the page back with notes. Once it is satisfied, the printed book (your program) is fast and reliable. (See Figure 1.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. Source code goes through the compiler. Mistakes stop here, before the program runs.

items: Here is the smallest complete Rust program.

Read it piece by piece. fn means function. main is the special name where the program starts. The parentheses hold inputs (none here). The curly braces hold the body. println! prints a line of text. The exclamation mark tells you it is a macro, a helper that writes code for you.
The semicolon ends the statement.
Printing values uses holes. Each {} in the text is filled by the next value you list after the string.
Some values have no plain text form, such as a tuple or a list. For those you ask for the debug form with {:?}. You can also name a value inside the braces like {name}.

Real projects use Cargo. Typing cargo new hello makes a folder with a main.rs file. cargo run builds and runs it. cargo build only builds. cargo check only checks for errors, which is the fastest way to get feedback. In our lab you skip all of that: just press Run.

Now the most important skill: reading errors. Rust errors have a code such as E0382, an arrow pointing at a line and column, and often a help line. Read from the top. Fix the first error first, because later ones are often just echoes of it.
Comments start with two slashes and are ignored by the compiler. Use them to explain why, not what.
Memory trick: Write, Check, Run. Write the code, the compiler Checks it, then you Run it.

chapters.title: Variables, types and values

maps.title: Variables

summary: A variable is a named box that holds a value. In Rust the boxes are locked by default: you must say mut if you want to change one. This one choice makes programs easier to reason about.
Every value has a type, which tells Rust how much memory it takes and what you may do with it. Rust usually works out the type for you, but it never silently turns one type into another.
You will learn let, mut, shadowing, whole numbers, decimals, booleans, characters, tuples and arrays, and what happens when a number gets too big.

A fixed group of values of possibly different types.
A number going past the largest value its type can hold.

keyPoints: let makes a fixed variable; let mut makes a changeable one.

ELI5. Think of labelled boxes. By default a box is glued shut after you put something in. If you want to change it later, you must say so when you make it, with mut. If you want a different kind of thing in a box with the same label, you make a new box with that label and hide the old one.

Now the real words. let makes a variable that cannot change. let mut makes it changeable. Shadowing makes a new variable with the same name. Every value has a type such as i32 for whole numbers or f64 for decimals, and Rust never mixes types silently. Numbers have fixed ranges, so going past the top is overflow.
Try it. In the lab, make a changeable counter, then try to add a u8 over 255 and fix it with saturating_add.
If you remember one thing: locked by default, explicit conversions, fixed ranges.

Imagine labelled boxes on a shelf. let x = 5; puts the number 5 in a box labelled x and then locks the box. Try x = 6 and the compiler says you cannot assign twice to an immutable variable. If you want to change it, you say let mut x = 5;. (See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. A locked box, a changeable box, and shadowing, which makes a new box with the same name.

items: Why lock by default? When you read a program, a locked variable cannot change behind your back. You only need to look at where it was created. Changeable variables are marked, so you know where to be careful.
Shadowing is different from mut. It makes a brand new variable that reuses the name. Because it is new, it can even have a different type, which is handy for converting text to a number.

Types. The whole-number types are named by sign and size: i8, i16, i32, i64 (signed, can be negative) and u8, u16, u32, u64 (unsigned, zero or more). usize is used for sizes and positions. The default for a plain number is i32. Decimals are f64 by default.
Then there are bool (true or false) and char (one Unicode character, in single quotes). (See Figure 2.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.2. Each integer type has a fixed range. Going past it is overflow.

items: Rust will not mix types behind your back. An i32 times an f64 is an error, because it is unclear which type the answer should be. You choose, using as: a as f64 turns the integer into a decimal first.

Overflow. A u8 holds 0 to 255. Adding 10 to 250 would give 260, which does not fit. In a debug build Rust panics, which means the program stops with a message. If you want the answer to stop at the maximum, use saturating_add. If you want it to wrap around, use wrapping_add.
If you want to find out whether it fit, use checked_add, which returns an Option.

Compound types. A tuple groups values: let p = (3, 4.5, true). You reach inside with a dot and a position, p.0. An array holds several values of the same type and a fixed length: let a = [1, 2, 3]. Index with a[0]. Going past the end is a panic, never a quiet bug.
Memory trick: Locked unless mut. A box is Locked unless you say mut, and shadowing makes a New box.

chapters.title: Functions and control flow

maps.title: Control flow
links: loop | can | break with a value

summary: Programs make decisions and repeat things. Rust has if, match (later), and three kinds of loops. In Rust, if and blocks are expressions, which means they produce values.
Functions give names to pieces of work. Their parameters must have types, and the return type comes after an arrow.
The last line of a block without a semicolon is the value of the block. This is the most surprising habit for newcomers, and the most useful once you get used to it.

glossary.def: A named piece of reusable code.
An input to a function, with a type.
Code that produces a value.
Code that does something but gives no value.
A sequence like 1..=5.

keyPoints: Functions need typed parameters and an arrow for the return type.
The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.
if is an expression and needs a bool condition.
for iterates a range or collection; while checks a condition; loop runs until break.
break can carry a value out of a loop.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Variables, types and values:
• let makes a fixed variable; let mut makes a changeable one.
• Shadowing makes a new variable and can change the type.

• Integer types have fixed ranges; overflow panics.
• Tuples group mixed values; arrays hold same-typed values.
ELI5. A function is a recipe card. You give it ingredients and it gives back a dish. And in Rust the dish is just the last line of the recipe, with no full stop.

Now the real words. A function has a name, typed parameters, and a return type after an arrow. The last expression, without a semicolon, is the value returned. if is also an expression, so it can produce a value. Loops come in three kinds: for visits items, while repeats while something is true, loop repeats until break.
Try it. Write FizzBuzz in the lab, testing the both case first.
If you remember one thing: no semicolon on the last line means: this is the answer.
Start with functions. A function is a named recipe. You give it ingredients (parameters), and it hands back a dish (the return value).
Look closely at square. There is no return word and no semicolon after n * n. That is on purpose. A block ends with its last expression, and that expression is the value.
If you add a semicolon, you turn it into a statement, the block gives nothing, and the compiler complains that it expected an i32. You can still write return n * n; when you want to leave early.
Conditions. if checks a true-or-false value. Unlike some languages, Rust never treats numbers as truthy, so if n is an error but if n > 0 is fine.
Because if is an expression, both branches must give the same type. That is why the example above can store the result straight into kind. (See Figure 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. The four basic shapes of control flow.

items: Loops. for i in 1..=5 visits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (the equals sign includes the end; 1..5 stops before 5). while n < 10 repeats while the condition is true. loop repeats forever until you break, and break can hand back a value.
continue skips to the next round. Loops can be given labels to break out of a nested loop, but you will rarely need that early on.
Put it together with FizzBuzz: count from 1 to 15, printing Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for 5, and FizzBuzz for both. The only trick is to test the combined case first.

chapters.title: Ownership: who owns the data?

maps.title: Ownership
links: Ownership | says | One owner per value
One owner per value | stored on | Stack handle
Stack handle | points to | Heap data
Ownership transfers | for String | Old name is dead
Ownership transfers | not for | Copy types
Drop | happens at | End of scope
Old name is dead | gives | Error E0382

summary: Ownership is the idea that makes Rust different. Every value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is cleaned up. You never free memory by hand, and you never forget to.
Assigning or passing a value to another variable moves ownership. The old variable can no longer be used. Simple types like numbers are copied instead.
The compiler checks all of this before the program runs, which is why Rust programs can be both fast and safe.

glossary.def: The variable responsible for a value.
Transferring ownership; the old variable is no longer valid.
Types that are duplicated instead of moved, such as integers.
An explicit deep copy made with .clone().
Cleanup that runs when an owner goes out of scope.
Memory for data whose size can change, such as a String.

keyPoints: One value, one owner.
Assigning a String moves it; numbers are copied.
Use .clone() when you really want a second copy.
Values are dropped when the owner leaves scope, in reverse order.
Error E0382 means you used a moved value.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Functions and control flow:
• Functions need typed parameters and an arrow for the return type.
• The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.
• if is an expression and needs a bool condition.
• for iterates a range or collection; while checks a condition; loop runs until break.
• break can carry a value out of a loop.

ELI5. You have one library book with your name on it. If you give it to a friend, it is theirs now and you cannot read it. If you want both of you to read it, you make a photocopy. When you leave the library for good, your books are returned automatically.

Now the real words. Each value has one owner. Assigning a String to another variable moves it, so the old variable is dead. Numbers are copied instead. clone makes an explicit copy. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped, last created first. Using a moved value is error E0382.
Try it. In the lab, move a String into another variable and use the old one to see E0382, then fix it with clone. Watch the Ownership log.
If you remember one thing: one value, one owner, the owner cleans up.

Picture a library book. Only one person can have it checked out at a time. If you hand it to a friend, you do not have it any more. That is a move. If you photocopy the book first, you both have one. That is clone.

First, where data lives. Small fixed-size values such as numbers sit on the stack, a fast tidy pile. Things that can grow, like a String, keep a small handle on the stack with a pointer, length and capacity, and the real characters on the heap. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. A String is a stack handle that owns bytes on the heap.

items: After let s2 = s1, the handle was copied to s2 and s1 gave up ownership. If both kept it, they would each try to free the same heap bytes when they left scope, which is a classic bug. Rust avoids it by making only one of them valid. If you then print s1, you get the error borrow of moved value.
(See Figure 4.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.2. A move: s2 now owns the data and s1 is dead.

items: Numbers are different. let a = 5; let b = a; copies the 5, because copying a small number is cheap and safe, so both stay valid. Types that behave this way implement a trait called Copy: integers, floats, bool, char, and tuples of Copy things.

Passing to a function also moves. If shout takes a String, calling shout(s) hands s over. Afterwards main cannot use s unless the function gives it back by returning it, or you used clone, or (next chapter) you borrowed instead. (See Figure 4.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.3. Values are dropped at the end of their scope, last created first.

items: Drop. When an owner leaves its scope, Rust calls drop on the value, freeing the heap memory. You can even write your own Drop code to print a message or close a file. The order is the reverse of creation: the last variable made is the first one cleaned up.
The Ownership log under your lab output shows moves and drops as they happen.

Clone makes an independent deep copy: let t = s.clone();. It costs time and memory, so Rust makes you ask for it explicitly. A good habit: when you see E0382, first ask whether you really need a second owner, or whether a borrow (next chapter) is enough.
Memory trick: One owner, then Drop. One owner at a time; when the owner leaves, the value is Dropped, last in first out.

chapters.title: Borrowing and references

maps.title: Borrowing
links: Two rules | enforced by | The compiler
Two rules | end at | Last use
The compiler | reports | E0502 and E0499

summary: Often you want to use a value without taking it over. You do that by borrowing: you pass a reference, written with an ampersand. The owner keeps the value, and you just look at it, or change it if the reference is mutable.

The borrowing rules are short: at any moment you may have any number of shared references, or exactly one mutable reference, but never both. The compiler enforces this, which prevents data races and surprise changes.
References always point at valid data. Slices are a special kind of reference to part of a string or list.

glossary.def: A borrowed view of a value, written &x.
&T: read only, many allowed.
&mut T: can change, only one at a time.
A reference to part of a string or array.
Using * to reach the value a reference points to.
Non-lexical lifetimes: a borrow ends at its last use.

keyPoints: & borrows; the owner keeps ownership.
Many readers OR one writer.
A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the block.
&mut needs a let mut variable.
&str is a slice: a borrowed piece of a string.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Ownership: who owns the data?:
• One value, one owner.
• Assigning a String moves it; numbers are copied.
• Use .clone() when you really want a second copy.
• Values are dropped when the owner leaves scope, in reverse order.
• Error E0382 means you used a moved value.
ELI5. Borrowing is reading a library book in the reading room. Many people can read the same book at the same time. But if someone wants to write notes in it, everyone else must step away first.

Now the real words. A reference is written with &. You can have many shared references (&T), or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T), never both. A borrow lasts until its last use. Slices like &str are references to part of a string. Rust checks all this before your program runs.
Try it. In the lab, pass a String to a function by reference, then try two &mut at once and read E0499.
If you remember one thing: many readers or one writer.

Back to the library. Borrowing is like reading a book in the library without taking it home. Many people can read the same book at once. But if one person wants to scribble in it, nobody else can be reading at that moment.
The function asks for &String, a reference. The caller passes &s. After the call, main still owns s and can print it. No clone, no moving back and forth. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. Many shared readers, or one mutable writer.

items: To change something through a reference, both the variable and the reference must say mut: let mut s, and &mut s, and the function takes &mut String.

The big rule again: many & or one &mut, never both at once. Why? Imagine reading a list while someone else is deleting items from it. You would see nonsense. Rust prevents that situation at compile time. The error is E0502 (reader and writer mixed) or E0499 (two writers).

How long does a borrow last? Until the last time you use the reference. This is called non-lexical lifetimes. So you can read through a reference, finish with it, and then start a mutable borrow right after.

The classic broken example takes a reference to the first item of a Vec, then pushes onto the Vec, then uses the reference. Moving the print before the push fixes it, because the reference is finished by then.

Why does a push cause trouble? A Vec may need to move to bigger memory when it grows. A reference to the old spot would then point at nothing. By refusing the code, Rust saves you from a dangling pointer. (See Figure 5.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.2. A slice is a view into part of a string.

items: Slices. &s[0..5] borrows the first five bytes of s. The type of a string slice is &str, and it is also the type of string literals like "hello". Prefer &str in function parameters, because it accepts both String borrows and literals.
While a slice exists, the original cannot be changed, for the same reason as above.

A rule of thumb for choosing: pass by reference (&T) when the function only needs to look, &mut T when it must change the value, and by value (T) when the function should take over ownership, for example to store it.
Memory trick: Many readers or one writer. Many Readers OR one Writer, never both.

summary: An enum is a type that can be exactly one of several variants. Each variant can carry its own data. Combined with match, enums let you describe choices precisely and have the compiler check that you handled them all.
Rust has no null. Instead it has Option, an enum with Some(value) and None, so the type itself tells you when a value might be missing.

ELI5. A traffic light is exactly one of red, yellow or green. An enum is a type like that. Match is the rule book: for each colour, what do you do? The rule book must cover every colour or the compiler will not let you drive.

Now the real words. An enum value is one of its variants, and variants may carry data. match compares a value to patterns and must be exhaustive. Option is an enum: Some(value) or None. That is how Rust avoids null. if let handles one case.
Try it. Delete a match arm in the lab and read which case the compiler says you missed.
If you remember one thing: an enum is one of several, and match makes you handle them all.
Think about a traffic light. It is always exactly one of red, yellow or green. An enum models that: you list the possible states, and a value holds exactly one.

The key feature of match is that it must be exhaustive. If you delete the Green arm, the program will not compile and the error tells you which variant you missed. When you later add a fourth colour to the enum, every match that does not handle it fails to compile.
The compiler finds every place you need to update.
Variants can carry data, and each variant can carry a different shape of data. (See Figure 7.1 below.)

items: Patterns bind names. In Shape::Circle(r), the radius is bound to the name r for use in that arm. You can also match ranges (90..=100), alternatives (1 | 2), and add a guard with if: n if n < 0 => ... .

A function that might not find something returns an Option, and the compiler makes you handle the None case before you use the value. (See Figure 7.2 below.)

Strings need extra care because they are UTF-8: a character can be more than one byte.

ELI5. A Vec is a train that can add carriages. A String is a train of letters. A HashMap is a coat check: hand in a ticket (the key) and get your coat (the value).

Now the real words. Vec grows with push and is read by index, with get for a safe Option. Indexing past the end panics. String is UTF-8, so len counts bytes and chars counts letters. HashMap stores key-value pairs, and entry with or_insert is the way to count things.

A Vec is like a train that can add carriages. All carriages hold the same kind of thing, and each has a number starting at zero. (See Figure 8.1 below.)

Strings. String::from("hi") makes an owned, growable String. push_str adds text, push adds one character, and + joins (it takes ownership of the left side). format! builds a new string without moving anything, which is usually easiest.

HashMap. Use it to count things or look things up. entry gives you a slot, and or_insert fills it if it was empty. The star dereferences the reference to the number inside.

summary: Things go wrong: files are missing, text is not a number, networks fail. Rust splits problems into two kinds: bugs that should stop the program (panics) and expected problems that the caller can handle (Result).
Result is an enum with Ok(value) and Err(error). You must deal with both, either by matching, by providing a fallback, or by passing the error up with the question mark operator.
The type system makes error handling visible: if a function can fail, its signature says so.

An enum: Ok(value) or Err(error).
Takes the value or panics.
On Err, return it from the function; on Ok, take the value.

ELI5. A waiter who finds the kitchen is out of an ingredient does not burn down the restaurant. They come back and tell you so you can choose again. A Result is that message: here is your dish, or here is the problem.

Now the real words. A panic stops the program and is for bugs. A Result is Ok(value) or Err(error), for problems you expect. unwrap takes the value or panics. unwrap_or gives a default. The ? operator returns the error immediately or unwraps the value.
Try it. Write parse_age returning a Result, then shorten a two-match function with ?.
If you remember one thing: expected problems return Result; bugs panic.

When a restaurant is out of an ingredient, the waiter does not set the kitchen on fire. They come back and tell you, and you choose something else. A Result is that message: either here is your dish or sorry, here is the problem.
Panics. A panic prints a message, stops the program and exits with code 101. They happen for bugs such as an index out of range, dividing by zero, integer overflow, or calling unwrap on None.
Our lab prints the same message Rust would: thread main panicked at the line and column, then what went wrong.
Prefer a fallback such as unwrap_or when a default makes sense. Use unwrap only when it truly cannot fail, and expect("reason") when you want a clearer message.
Result. A function that can fail says so in its type: Result<u8, String> means it gives back a u8 or an error message. (See Figure 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. Result has two paths. The question mark follows the success path or returns the error.

items: The ? operator. Matching on every call gets long. Put ? after a call that returns a Result: on Ok it unwraps the value and continues; on Err it returns that error from your function immediately. The enclosing function must return a compatible Result.

In bigger programs you define your own error enum with a variant for each way things can fail, so callers can match on what went wrong. The same ideas apply: return Result, use ? to pass errors up, and decide at the top (usually main) what to tell the user.

ELI5. A library card works only while the library is open. If the library closes while you still hold the card, the card is useless. A lifetime is the time during which a reference is still valid.

Now the real words. A reference must never outlive its data, or it would dangle. Usually Rust works lifetimes out. When a function returns a reference chosen from several inputs, you name the relationship with 'a. Annotations describe; they do not change how long anything lives.
Try it. Fix longest by adding 'a, and fix a does not live long enough error by printing earlier.
If you remember one thing: references must not outlive what they point at.

Think of a library card that is valid only while the library is open. If the library closes while you still hold the card, the card is useless. A lifetime is that opening time, and Rust checks that your references never outlive it. (See Figure 11.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.1. The reference r lives longer than x, so the program is rejected.

items: This is rejected. x lives only inside the inner braces. After they close, x is dropped, but r still points at it. The compiler says x does not live long enough. The fix is to use r while x is still alive, or to keep x in a wider scope.

Functions. Consider longest, which returns whichever of two strings is longer. The result is a reference, but to which input? Rust cannot know, and refuses with missing lifetime specifier. You tell it with a lifetime name.

Read it as: for some lifetime a, both inputs live at least as long as a, and the result lives for a too. So the result is valid as long as both inputs are. The annotation does not stretch anything. It describes what is true so the compiler can check callers.

Elision. For simple functions Rust fills in lifetimes. With exactly one reference parameter, the output reference gets that lifetime. With &self methods, the output gets self's. That is why fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str needs no annotation, but longest with two inputs does.
Structs that borrow. A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime too: struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }. It means an Excerpt cannot outlive the text it points into.

Returning a reference to a local variable is always wrong: the local is dropped when the function ends. Rust reports missing lifetime specifier or cannot return reference to local variable. Return an owned String instead.
A good rule: if lifetimes are fighting you, ask whether the function should own its data rather than borrow it.
Memory trick: Never outlive. A reference must Never outlive what it points to; name it with 'a when inputs compete.

chapters.title: Closures and iterators
summary: A closure is a small anonymous function that can use variables from around it. An iterator is something that yields a sequence of values one at a time.
Together they let you describe what you want, such as keep the odd ones, square them, add them up, instead of writing a loop that spells out every step.
Iterators are lazy: nothing happens until something consumes them, and they compile down to loops as fast as handwritten ones.

glossary.def: An anonymous function written |x| x + 1.
A closure using a variable from its surroundings.
Something that produces values one by one.
A step like map or filter that makes a new iterator.
A step like sum or collect that produces a final result.
Doing nothing until asked for a value.

keyPoints: Closures are |args| body and can capture variables.
map transforms; filter keeps; sum, collect, count consume.
Iterator chains are lazy.
collect needs to know the target type.
iter borrows; into_iter consumes.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Lifetimes:
• A reference must not outlive its data.
• E0597: borrowed value does not live long enough.
• E0106: missing lifetime specifier on returned references.
• Name lifetimes to link inputs to outputs.
• Return owned values when in doubt.

ELI5. A conveyor belt carries items past machines. One machine removes the bad ones, another paints each one, and at the end a worker counts what arrives. Nothing moves until the worker at the end asks for the first item.

Now the real words. A closure is a small unnamed function like |x| x + 1 that can use variables around it. Iterators yield values one at a time. Adapters like map and filter make new iterators, consumers like sum and collect finish the job. Chains are lazy.
Try it. Sum the squares of the odd numbers from 1 to 10 in one chain: 165.
If you remember one thing: describe what you want; the chain does the looping.
A closure is a function without a name that you can hand around like a note. Where a normal function cannot see the variables of the code that calls it, a closure can capture them.
The closure add uses n from outside. The pipes hold the parameters. You will mostly write closures as short arguments to iterator methods.

An iterator is like a conveyor belt. Items ride along, and you attach machines: a filter that removes items, a map that changes each one. Finally a consumer at the end collects what arrives. (See Figure 12.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.1. A source, two adapters and a consumer.

items: Here the range is the source. filter keeps the odd ones. map squares them. sum adds them to 165. Notice that the machines only start moving when sum asks for values. That is laziness, and it means an iterator chain does no wasted work.

Common adapters: map, filter, enumerate (adds positions), zip (pairs two iterators), take, skip, rev, chain. Common consumers: sum, count, min, max, fold (your own accumulator), any, all, find, position, collect.
collect builds a collection from an iterator. It needs to know which one, so you give the type: Vec<String>, HashMap, String, or even Result<Vec<_>, _>, which stops at the first error.

iter() borrows the items. into_iter() takes them. iter_mut() lets you change them in place. Which one you use follows the ownership rules from earlier chapters: if you still need the collection afterwards, borrow it.
Memory trick: Source, adapt, consume. Source, Adapt with map and filter, Consume with sum or collect.

maps.title: Smart pointers
links: Smart pointers | include | Rc and Arc
Rc and Arc | give | Shared ownership
RefCell | checks | Borrow rules at run time

summary: Smart pointers are types that act like references but also own data and add abilities. Box puts a value on the heap. Rc lets several owners share a value and counts them. RefCell lets you change a value through a shared handle by checking the borrowing rules at run time.

Rust also helps with threads. The same ownership and borrowing rules that prevent memory bugs also prevent data races: if your program compiles, two threads cannot accidentally write the same data at once.
This chapter closes the course with a map of where to go next.

glossary.def: A pointer to one value on the heap.
Reference counted pointer: many owners, single thread.
Atomic Rc: many owners across threads.
Interior mutability: borrow rules checked at run time.
A unit of work that runs alongside others.
A queue for sending values between threads.

keyPoints: Box<T> owns one heap value; needed for recursive types.
Rc<T> shares ownership; Rc::clone adds an owner.
RefCell<T> allows change through a shared reference, checked at run time.
Channels move data between threads.
Rc is not thread safe: use Arc.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Closures and iterators:
• Closures are |args| body and can capture variables.
• map transforms; filter keeps; sum, collect, count consume.
• Iterator chains are lazy.
• collect needs to know the target type.
• iter borrows; into_iter consumes.

ELI5. A Box is a single locker. Rc is a locker with several keys and a counter on the door: when the last key is handed back, the locker is emptied. RefCell is a locker with a sign-out sheet checked while you use it, not before.

Now the real words. Box puts one value on the heap, and lets recursive types work. Rc shares ownership and counts owners. RefCell moves the borrow check to run time. Threads run work side by side, channels move values between them, and Arc is the thread-safe Rc.
Try it. Share a vector between two Rc handles and push through one of them.
If you remember one thing: Box owns, Rc shares, RefCell allows change through a share.
Box. A recursive type such as a list that contains another list would have infinite size, since each contains the next. A Box is a fixed-size pointer to the heap, which breaks the loop.

Rc. Sometimes one value truly has several owners, like a node in a graph. Rc keeps a count of owners. Rc::clone does not copy the data, it adds one to the count. When the count reaches zero, the data is freed. (See Figure 13.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.1. Box owns one value. Rc counts owners. RefCell allows changes through a shared handle.

items: RefCell. Shared handles are read only. RefCell moves the borrow check to run time so you can change the contents anyway: borrow() reads and borrow_mut() writes. If you break the rules (two borrow_mut at once) the program panics instead of failing to compile.
The common pairing Rc<RefCell<T>> means shared and changeable.

Threads. thread::spawn runs a closure in another thread. join waits for it to finish. A channel lets threads talk: the sender tx sends, the receiver rx receives, and sending moves the value, so only one thread owns it at a time.
In this lab, threads run one after another so output is predictable, but the compiler rules are exactly the real ones. (See Figure 13.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.2. A worker sends a message through a channel to the main thread.

items: Rc is not allowed across threads because its counter is not atomic. If you try, the compiler says Rc cannot be sent between threads safely. Swap in Arc. For shared changeable data across threads, the standard pairing is Arc<Mutex<T>>.

Where next? Read the official book, The Rust Programming Language, which is free online. Practise with small exercises such as Rustlings. Try cargo new on your own computer and build a command-line tool. Explore crates on crates.io.
Rust rewards patience: the compiler errors you saw here are the same ones professionals fix every day.
